title: 2 Chronicles 2:11–18
context: Huram king of Tyre answers Solomon in writing. He blesses the LORD, the God of Israel, who made heaven and earth, and sends “a skillful man, endowed with understanding, Huram-abi,” the son of a woman of the daughters of Dan, whose father was a man of Tyre. The already drafted 1 Kings 7:13–14 notes record a parallel craftsman named Hiram, “the son of a widow of the tribe of Naphtali,” whose father was a man of Tyre, and they warn against confusing him with Hiram, or Huram, the king. WEB spelling in this chapter is Huram-abi; the two accounts should be named and not forced into one genealogy. Huram accepts the wheat, barley, oil, and wine, and promises timber floated to Joppa, to be carried up to Jerusalem. Solomon then counts the foreigners in the land and assigns them as in 2:2. As in 2:1–10, WEB numbering for this chapter runs one verse ahead of the common Hebrew division, because WEB 2:1 is Hebrew 1:18; the notes keep the WEB numbers. Both traditions treat the letter, the craftsman, and the labor counts as historical report, consistent with the drafted 1 Kings 5 and 7 notes, and invent no party contrast over the names or the numbers.

verses.text: Then Huram the king of Tyre answered in writing, which he sent to Solomon, “Because the LORD loves his people, he has made you king over them.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Huram answers in writing, “Because the LORD loves his people, he has made you king over them.” The Tyrian king reads Solomon’s throne as a sign of the LORD’s love for Israel. The already drafted 1 Kings 5 correspondence has Hiram rejoice and bless the LORD in related terms, though not in this exact sentence.

Arminian readers hear a real confession from a neighboring king, love named as the reason Solomon sits on the throne.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also start from the LORD’s love for his people as the cause of the kingship, spoken here by Huram and written down.

Both traditions take the verse as praise of the LORD’s care for Israel, not as a party argument about the foreign king’s faith.

verses.text: Huram continued, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who made heaven and earth, who has given to David the king a wise son, endowed with discretion and understanding, who would build a house for the LORD and a house for his kingdom.
verses.arminianNotes:
Huram continues, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who made heaven and earth, who has given to David the king a wise son, endowed with discretion and understanding, who would build a house for the LORD and a house for his kingdom.” The blessing names the LORD as maker of heaven and earth and recognizes the wisdom already given, the same two houses Solomon named in 2:1.

Arminian readers hear Huram blessing Israel’s God and acknowledging a wise son given to David, a public recognition of the gift of 1:12.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the wisdom is a gift from the LORD who made heaven and earth, and that the two houses are named again in the same terms as 2:1.

Both traditions read the blessing as shared ground with the gift of wisdom, without a contrast over Huram’s words.

verses.text: Now I have sent a skillful man, endowed with understanding, Huram-abi,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now I have sent a skillful man, endowed with understanding, Huram-abi,” WEB’s spelling in this verse. He is the craftsman Solomon had asked for in 2:7. 1 Kings 7:13–14 later names a craftsman Hiram brought out of Tyre. The two names and the two settings should be reported side by side; the man should not be confused with Huram the king.

Arminian readers take the sending as the answer to the request, a real craftsman on the way, under the name this book gives him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stay consistent with the drafted 1 Kings 7 notes, which already distinguish the craftsman from the king and record the name difference without forcing a single spelling.

Both traditions use WEB “Huram-abi” here and leave the parallel in 1 Kings 7 unharmonized.

verses.text: the son of a woman of the daughters of Dan; and his father was a man of Tyre. He is skillful to work in gold, in silver, in bronze, in iron, in stone, in timber, in purple, in blue, in fine linen, and in crimson, also to engrave any kind of engraving and to devise any device, that there may be a place appointed to him with your skillful men, and with the skillful men of my lord David your father.
verses.arminianNotes:
He is “the son of a woman of the daughters of Dan; and his father was a man of Tyre.” 1 Kings 7:14 says he was “the son of a widow of the tribe of Naphtali,” and that his father was a man of Tyre, a worker in bronze. The father’s Tyrian origin agrees; the mother’s tribe is named differently, Dan here and Naphtali there. The difference should be named, not erased by a theory the verses do not state.

Arminian readers keep both identifications in view and refuse to rewrite one line from the other.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave Dan and Naphtali unharmonized, as the drafted 1 Kings 7 notes already do, and they note the wide range of skills listed here, not bronze alone.

Both traditions treat the genealogy as a reported difference, not as a doctrinal fork.

verses.text: “Now therefore, the wheat, the barley, the oil, and the wine which my lord has spoken of, let him send to his servants;
verses.arminianNotes:
Huram accepts “the wheat, the barley, the oil, and the wine which my lord has spoken of,” and asks that they be sent to his servants. The list matches the goods of 2:10, though this verse does not repeat the quantities. The agreement is the other half of the offer in Solomon’s letter.

Arminian readers hear a real acceptance of the provisions, the trade going both ways as the letters have stated.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also read a straightforward contract: the food and drink named in 2:10 are to be sent, and the next verse will promise the timber in return.

Both traditions keep the verse in the register of the correspondence, without a contrast over the goods.

verses.text: and we will cut wood out of Lebanon, as much as you need. We will bring it to you in rafts by sea to Joppa; then you shall carry it up to Jerusalem.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Huram’s servants will “cut wood out of Lebanon, as much as you need.” They will bring it “in rafts by sea to Joppa”; and Solomon is to carry it up to Jerusalem. 1 Kings 5:8–9 has a similar arrangement, timber brought by sea to the place Solomon chooses. Joppa is named here as the landing.

Arminian readers take the route as a practical plan, rafts to Joppa and then the climb to Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also name the parallel and the added port. The timber comes as far as Joppa by sea; the last stage is Solomon’s to carry up.

Both traditions leave the two descriptions unmerged and invent no symbolism in the rafts or the port.

verses.text: Solomon counted all the foreigners who were in the land of Israel, after the census with which David his father had counted them; and they found one hundred fifty-three thousand six hundred.
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon counts “all the foreigners who were in the land of Israel, after the census with which David his father had counted them; and they found one hundred fifty-three thousand six hundred.” The total is the sum of the three groups in 2:18. 1 Kings 5:13 records a levy of thirty thousand from all Israel that is not stated in the same way here; this verse describes the counted workers as foreigners, after David’s census. The already drafted 1 Kings 5:15 notes already mention that 2 Chronicles 2:17–18 describes these workers as foreigners.

Arminian readers take the census notice as a historical count, not as a hidden lesson in the number.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stay consistent with those Kings notes. The 153,600 are foreigners in this account; the thirty thousand levy of 1 Kings 5:13 is a separate notice, not to be forced into this verse.

Both traditions name the difference of description and refuse to turn the total into a symbol.

verses.text: He set seventy thousand of them to bear burdens, eighty thousand who were stone cutters in the mountains, and three thousand six hundred overseers to assign the people their work.
verses.arminianNotes:
He set “seventy thousand of them to bear burdens, eighty thousand who were stone cutters in the mountains, and three thousand six hundred overseers to assign the people their work.” The figures repeat 2:2 and add that the overseers assign the work. 1 Kings 5:15–16 has the same bearer and cutter counts, but “three thousand three hundred” chief officers. As before, the already drafted Kings notes treat the overseer difference as a question of counting, not of doctrine.

Arminian readers name both overseer totals again and leave them unharmonized.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers do the same, consistent with 1 Kings 5:16 as already drafted. Seventy thousand and eighty thousand agree; three thousand six hundred here is not the same figure as three thousand three hundred there.

Both traditions close the chapter on that unforced report of the labor force, with no party contrast over the numbers.
